en: Having prostrated before the Lord of Ganas, who is adorned with matted locks and praised by Vāgīśa and others,
as well as the Lord of Speech and the Lord of Śrī, the giver of boons to the worlds; 1.

One should pronounce two words sequentially, then out of sequence, and then in reverse order, along with their phonetic characteristics; at every junction [of words], this is called *jaṭā* by the wise.
Its measurement is found in the first chapter (*prapāṭhaka*) of the *Prātiśākhya*.
Even when there is the substitution of the letter *r*, it is not [considered] a *dhāma* because of the word "and" (*ca*) in the Vedic term;
in the three sequences, there is an eightfold junction (*saṃdhi*), with two each at the beginning and the end.
Here, the junctions are designated as Vedic (*ārṣa*) within their own [categories], while others are non-Vedic (*anārṣaka*).
Elsewhere, there are five types of euphonic junction (*sandhi*); among them, where the vowels and consonants are identical, that is the single *sandhi* known as *ārṣaka*.
One should speak of it as having two words, six words, or likewise nine words.

In the specific case of the distinction between vowels and consonants, one proceeds through the triple sequence in due order. Having ascended to the three words in the triple sequence along with the euphonic junctions, one descends according to the rule; this is known as the "re-ascension."

That which is indeed seen in the sūtras at the joints [of the system] when they are not inverted; that which is favored by logic; and that which is [established] through examples—that is what is called [the definitive teaching].
Wherever it is distinguished by the power of the connection between the meaning of the sūtra and logic, [that is the definitive meaning].
When [the pause] occurs in reverse order according to the rule, it is designated as *sandhi*.

It is traditionally taught that the third [syllable] of the principal [verse], starting from the three-footed [meter], is the first three-footed unit in the verses and Brāhmaṇa passages. Indeed, in those cases, the first three-footed unit alone [is so designated]. 9–10.

The maxim beginning with "the three-footed" applies to cases of elision and non-elision; therein, if that which stands [in the rule] is connected with another, the preceding grammatical operation does not take place. For a word is indeed formed by aiming at one specific element.
But that which is not accepted elsewhere by those who favor the *jaṭā* [tradition],
which many students do not recite as it is obtained through the rules like the *saṃhitā*,
is called the *bāhvādṛta* at the time of the *jaṭā*. 12–13.
When an extraordinary sandhi occurs in the *jaṭā* that would not arise [in the standard form],
it is called the "example of the sandhi taught in the *Brāhmaṇa-araṇyaka*. Likewise, in the case of *brāhmaṇāya* and *itya*, there is the phonetic combination (*akṣara-saṃhitā*) of *ityopa*.
Even there, because of the predominance of the preceding [element], the single vowel *ai* would not occur here;
since the substitution of *ṣ* for *ś* would have been obtained, and then the phoneme *n* remains as the remainder of the letter,
the original *n* follows from that— thus it is established that "he struck down Vṛtra" (*śnathad vṛtram*).
But when there is a negation of the cause, there is no injunction by the force of that cause;
in the case of the cognition of the word *īṅya*, the injunction does not partake of the negation.
Furthermore, just as the injunction of existence (*satva*) is not desired by the force of the *kṛt* suffix, [so it is here].
Furthermore, because this [suffix] is predominant, it serves as the cause for the application of the rule *kṛdher* (Pāṇini 8.2.31).
Where there is *mahisṛjya* or *ṛtvant*, the substitution of *ṣ* does not occur in *pauruṣa* due to the prohibition concerning forms ending in *ṛt*, and because we observe the form *mahisapta*.
When "iḍasparidhi" is uttered, it serves to prohibit the mixing [of vowels];
therein, even for that which has the vowel *iṅ*, there may be more than one [instance], and likewise for "viśvāyuḥ.
In the case of "stomāya jyotiḥ," the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* does not occur.
Since it was previously unobstructed, such being the case, there is a state of being pierced.
When there is no prior prohibition, a counter-exception is not recorded; for that which possesses a counter-exception, it is only when it ends in *ṣat*, and not otherwise. 21–22.
If *la* follows a *ṭa*-class consonant (*ṭavarga*), it becomes difficult to pronounce;
otherwise, it would contradict [the rule] because of the absence of doubling (*dvitva*) and the presence of a pause (*virāma*).
In this context, the term "non-Vedic" (*anārṣa*) is employed in the formulation of the *saṃhitā* rule.
In the case of *jaṭā*, however, the original form (*prakṛti*) should prevail at the beginning and the end because it is of Vedic origin (ārṣa).

Wherever [a change] is observed other than in the cases of *atvara* and *ep*— such as the substitution of *ṣ* for *s* (*ṣatva*) and *ṇ* for *n* (*ṇatva*) and so forth— it should be applied everywhere according to the regular order (*anuloma*).

For if the *yatva* and *repha* belong to that very [word] which is followed by a vowel in its Vedic form (ārṣa), then when it exists in its human (pauruṣa) form followed by a vowel, there is likewise a prohibition; otherwise it would not be so.
If the term "two-word" (*dvipada*) is used either as a primary factor (*pradhāna*) or as a cause (*nimitta*).
In the case of a transposition (*vyutkrama*), [the elision] is to be understood from all sides; in the case of a regular sequence (*krama*), it is from one part.
When there is an elision (*lopa*), those that remain stand as one, and thus they grasp it as a single unit.
Therefore, the final elision does not depend upon a cause (*nimitta*). 27–28.

Just as the elision of the word *anvi* occurs in the *saṃhitā*, so too does its elision occur in the *jaṭā*; however, there is no elision of *nya* anywhere. Even when joined with a long vowel in reverse order, it shall not possess the nature of a short vowel.
Likewise, when a cause is present, it is not prescriptive;

for instance, in the *pauruṣa* [Sūkta], there is no word ending in *k* or *p* due to that cause, such as in the case of the words *anuṣṭubh* and *triṣṭubh*, where one says "you are the *anuṣṭubh*. (30–31)
In the word *udadhi*, the long vowel (*dīrgha*) serves as an indicator (*upalakṣaka*) for the short vowel (*hrasva*);
likewise, in the word *prapara*, the short vowel indicates the long vowel.
Whatever [rule] is not seen in the thirty-two sūtras is established by the force of another sūtra.
Even that which is not explicitly stated is accepted from another source when it is obstructed;
as, for instance, in the case of a contradiction, [the rule] "pāravatī" and so forth is accepted based on what was said by the mother.
However, in the previous case, for the sake of establishing the two *tu* suffixes, when the elision of all [suffixes] has occurred, [the rule] remains. 33–34.
When *stha* follows *udaḥ*, there is elision (*salopa*) of the *s*; however, when *tam* follows, there is no elision of the *m*.
When *rājate* follows, both forms—*klibantau* (with elision) and *rājatau* (without elision)—occur.
This has been indicated without distinction because these [forms] are well-established among them.

Even when those very [rules] are omitted, others are not considered to be in proximity (savidha). From a combined [vowel], a long vowel arises; from a single phoneme (varṇa), there is a guṇa substitute; and that [guṇa] follows the phoneme.
Furthermore, the state of "not eating grass" (anatṛṇatva) is employed in the sense of "having taken hold of another food. (36–37)

For although [the rule] beginning with "pāryādi" prescribes the prefix *pra*, they do not actually say so; rather, a wise person should apply the change of *na* to *ṇa* for the word *upūrva*, because the correct phonetic form (*yathāvaṇṇam*) is not observed for the letter *ṭa* following the prefix *pra*.
38. This is because the correct phonetic form is not observed for the letter *ṭa* following the prefix *pra*.
The *satva* substitution occurs even when preceded by the letter *ā*, as seen in the example *agnāstve*;
likewise, the *apad* (non-pause) sandhi occurs after *api*, as seen in the example *apacchiṣṭa*; and the *anusvāra* is also obligatory when situated within a single word in all cases.

Furthermore, because there is an absence of a beginning and so forth, and because it is impermanent and redundant, the subsequent [phrase] "consisting of five words" (pañcapadam) is also to be understood as being as before; thus it should be known by the wise in all cases. 41.
The *krama* method should be understood as being like the *saṃhitā*, and the *jaṭā* and other such formations [should be understood] in the same way.
(42) In the case of the *ārṣa* [method], the *kārya* (the phonetic modification) occurs at the beginning and at the end; indeed, in other cases, it occurs on both sides.
O Āgnīdhra and Adhvaryu, when [a word] has been placed first, there may be elision even where there is no *saṃhitā*. (43)

If a portion of the *ārṣa* [text] has been lost, it is not otherwise composed by the wise; rather, in those places where there is no sūtra, that which exists in human works or in other texts is included here according to one's own discretion.
44. Just as it is in other books, so too is this treatise [arranged] at will.
Furthermore, by the word "again" (*punaḥ*) in the rule *kṛdhyuttare*, it is intended that [the rule] applies even in reverse order.
By the sūtra *nāddhvaraṃ ca*, the [application of the rule] to a syllable situated in the avagraha is prohibited.
When a vowel (*ac*) follows, a preceding *raṅga* (the letter *r*) is said to behave like a short vowel (*hrasva*). 45–46.

Just as a preceding long vowel becomes short when followed by *hali*, so too in the case of *manī* (in the word *manīṣā*), elision (*yalopa*) is desired due to the reversal [of the rule]; furthermore, because it is not found in the *saṃhitā* [reading], and because the eight [syllables] of the *mithuna* are observed. 47.
Surely they do not dance, for no one speaks loudly while another is speaking;
the letter *na* undergoes *ṇatva* when two globular sounds (*golaka*) are observed, as in the case of *pratilomaka*.
There are two kinds of word-composition (*padasaṃhitā*) regarding the syllables that constitute the limbs of a word. 48–49.

In this [work] consisting of various words, five *saṃhitās* are enjoined; where there might be *satva* and so forth due to a cause situated above the letters *ka* and *kha*, if the letter *kṣa* follows immediately, it undergoes that very rule and never otherwise. 50.
"Kramyārddhvanobhavatyagre pāpakorpayati" (51), and "viṣayoṃ'girah" as well as "apyagra" and so forth are elided;
"paritvā punarirjāyannaḥ sya rātīyata" is recorded [as a mantra]. (52)

O Agni, you are the protector of the seven-fold [sacrifice]; may you, the radiant one, shine upon us with splendor and brilliance; may the drop be joined again from its source. Flow on as the guardian of vows, beyond the sun, and likewise for the sake of higher knowledge.

He who, through the vital breath (*prāṇa*), bestows life—by what means does he place that *prāṇa* within me? (54) By what, O Agni, in this common dwelling, is the vigor of the path not lost? Through the application of the three-footed [meter] and so forth, there is the exercise of power. (55)
"Even when there is connection with another [word], it is always only *alopa* because of the explicit statement in the *Kaṇṭha* [text].
Thus ends the *Jaṭāvallī*.
